preamble: The shift from the near-open front vowel [æ] to the mid-central vowel [ə] (schwa) is a case of vowel reduction. In stress-timed English, /æ/ in a syllable that loses stress centralizes to [ə], producing alternations in derivationally related words (atom /ˈætəm/ ~ atomic /əˈtɒmɪk/), in unstressed compound elements, and in the weak forms of function words such as can, at, and, than. Few languages that reduce unstressed vowels to schwa also have a distinct /æ/, so the pattern is documented chiefly from English.

examples.note: When stress shifts to the second syllable, the first-syllable [æ] reduces to [ə].
The unstressed second element of the compound reduces [æ] to [ə].
Unstressed function words such as can, at, and, than reduce /æ/ to [ə] in connected speech.
The auxiliary takes the reduced form when unstressed before a verb.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Stress and vowel reduction in English. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_and_vowel_reduction_in_English
context: In unstressed syllables in English; conditioned by stress placement
